# `memcached`

`memcached` asks a memcached server for its statistics, over TCP, in
memcached's own text protocol. The check is healthy when the server gives
the requested statistics. The check also measures the server's connections,
how many items the server holds, and how full the cache is. A get is a
request to retrieve a cached item.

For the interval since the previous run, the check measures gets that found
an item and gets that found none. The check also measures the share of gets
that found an item and counts items removed to make room. MMWatchdog speaks
the protocol itself, so the node needs no separate memcached client program
for the check.

The value of the module is the server's address, written as host:port, such
as `127.0.0.1:11211`. The address has no default port, so a reader sees on
the check where it connects.

The check measures what the memcached server knows. Only the application
knows what the cache saves the application, such as database work caused by a miss.
A check of the application's own measures what the cache saves the application,
for example through a
[module of the project's own](../writing-modules.md).

## Inputs

The module takes one value, which a check writes after the module's name, and no other input.

- the value of `memcached` (string; required): The address of the memcached server, as host:port.

## Measurements

- `current_connections` (connections): The connections that are open to the server now.
- `cached_items` (items): The items that the server holds now.
- `cache_used_percent` (percent): The percentage of the server's configured cache memory used to store items.
- `cache_hits_per_second` (hits per second): The number of cache lookups per second since the previous run that found their item.
- `cache_misses_per_second` (misses per second): The number of cache lookups per second since the previous run that found no item, because the server never had the item, removed the item, or let the item expire.
- `cache_hit_percent` (percent): The percentage of cache lookups since the previous run that found an item, from 0 to 100. No reading is available without lookups.
- `cache_evictions_per_second` (evictions per second): The number of items per second removed before expiry to make room in the cache, measured since the previous run.

The module fails a check by itself, and it also reports these measurements. A check sets a limit on a measurement with `fail_when_measurement_above` or `fail_when_measurement_below`, and fails when a reading passes its limit. A check with the module always states an `alert_severity`. The configuration files reference explains limits in [checks that measure a number](../configuration-files.md#checks-that-measure).

## When the check fails, and when it cannot check

A run sends `stats` to the server and reads its answer, which ends with a
line that says `END`.

- **The check fails** when any of the following conditions occurs:
  - the connection does not open;
  - the server closes the connection before the answer is complete;
  - the answer does not arrive within the check group's
    `time_limit_per_run`;
  - the answer is not the statistics of a memcached server;
  - a reading is above a `fail_when_measurement_above` limit or below a
    `fail_when_measurement_below` limit.
- **MMWatchdog cannot check** when a limit names a measurement that this run could
  not make. The run is then unknown, with the reason:
  - the server gave no `curr_connections`, `curr_items`, or `limit_maxbytes`;
  - the server gave no `get_hits`, `get_misses`, `evictions`, or `uptime`,
    needed for hits, misses, hit ratio, and evictions;
  - no get reached the server since the run before, so there is no hit
    ratio (`cache_hit_percent`).

  Without a limit on an unavailable measurement, the run is healthy and
  omits the unavailable measurement's reading.

A failed run starts or continues the check's
[failing time](../../how-to/decide-when-a-check-alerts.md). An unknown run opens a
cannot-check incident of its own after the waiting times used for failure
incidents, as the
design's [failing time](../../changing-mmwatchdog/design/checks.md#the-failing-time)
describes.

## Examples

### The cache answers and has room

```yaml
# /etc/mmwatchdog/check_groups/cache.yml
check_groups:
  cache:
    check_every: 1m
    time_limit_per_run: 10s
    alert_after_failing_for: 3m
    recovered_after_healthy_for: 1m
    checks:
      cache_answers_and_has_room:
        memcached: 127.0.0.1:11211
        fail_when_measurement_above:
          cache_used_percent: 95
        alert_severity: warn
```

Every minute, MMWatchdog on the node opens a TCP connection to the memcached
server at `127.0.0.1:11211` and asks for statistics. The run is healthy when
the server answers and cached items occupy less than 95 percent of
memcached's configured capacity for storing items. The run's message is `cache_used_percent is 12.5 (fails above 95);
the memcached server at 127.0.0.1:11211 gave its statistics; hits, misses,
and evictions over 60.000s`. When the server does not answer, or the cache
is fuller than 95 percent, for 3 minutes, MMWatchdog sends a `warn` alert.

A memcached server whose cache is full is doing its job: it removes old
items to make room. So a limit on `cache_used_percent` says that the cache
is smaller than what the application would like to keep. The capacity concern is worth a
`warn`, not an `sos`. The measurements take a limit in the way that
every measurement does
([checks that measure a number](../configuration-files.md#checks-that-measure)).

### Most gets find their item

```yaml
# /etc/mmwatchdog/check_groups/cache.yml
check_groups:
  cache:
    check_every: 1m
    time_limit_per_run: 10s
    alert_after_failing_for: 10m
    recovered_after_healthy_for: 5m
    checks:
      most_gets_find_their_item:
        memcached: 127.0.0.1:11211
        fail_when_measurement_below:
          cache_hit_percent: 80              # of the gets in the minute since the run before
        fail_when_measurement_above:
          cache_evictions_per_second: 5      # items removed to make room, before they expired
        alert_severity: warn
```

Every minute, MMWatchdog on the node reads the memcached server's counters
and compares the counters with the previous run's counters. The run fails
when fewer than 80 percent of gets since the previous run found an item.
The run also fails when the server removed more than 5 items a second to
make room. The run's message is then, for example,
`cache_evictions_per_second is 0 (fails above 5);
cache_hit_percent is 42.5 (fails below 80); the memcached server at
127.0.0.1:11211 gave its statistics; hits, misses, and evictions over
60.000s`. After 10 minutes of such runs, MMWatchdog sends a `warn` alert.

Right after the server starts, its cache is cold: most gets find no item,
and `cache_hit_percent` is low. As the application fills the cache, the
share rises. The 10 minutes of `alert_after_failing_for` give a cache that
starts again time to warm up before anybody gets an alert. If the
application asks for nothing during the minute between runs, the check
cannot measure `cache_hit_percent` for the run ending the idle minute.
The limit on `cache_hit_percent` makes the run ending the idle minute
unknown, so set the hit-ratio limit on a cache the application uses all the
time.

## How it works

| Measurement | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `current_connections` | The server's `curr_connections`: the connections that are open to it now |
| `cached_items` | The server's `curr_items`: the items that it holds now |
| `cache_used_percent` | Bytes occupied by cached items (`bytes`) as a percent of the configured capacity for storing items (`limit_maxbytes`), 0 to 100 |
| `cache_hits_per_second` | The increase in the server's `get_hits`: gets that found an item |
| `cache_misses_per_second` | The increase in the server's `get_misses`: gets that found no item. The server never had the item, removed the item, or let the item expire. |
| `cache_hit_percent` | The hits as a percent of all gets since the run before, 0 to 100 |
| `cache_evictions_per_second` | The increase in the server's `evictions`: items removed to make room for new items, before expiration |

- **The hits, the misses, the hit ratio, and the evictions cover the time
  since the check's run before.** The server counts hits, misses, and
  evictions from the server's start. The check calculates rates and the
  hit ratio from counter increases between two runs. So the hit ratio of a
  cold cache differs from the hit ratio of a warm cache, whatever the server
  counted before.

  Three cases need two requests within a run: the first run, a run after a
  gap of more than `2 × check_every + time_limit_per_run`, and a run after
  the server started again. In each case, MMWatchdog asks the server a second
  time, 200 ms after the first request. The check calculates the rates and hit
  ratio from the counter increases between the two answers. So the check
  group's `time_limit_per_run` must be longer than `200ms`.

  The message ends with the interval covered by `cache_hits_per_second`,
  `cache_misses_per_second`, `cache_hit_percent`, and
  `cache_evictions_per_second`, such as `over 60.000s`.
  The [CPU sampling](../configuration-files.md#readings-over-a-time)
  section of the configuration files reference gives the rules that every module that
  measures a rate shares.
- **MMWatchdog sees that the server started again** when one of its counters, or its
  `uptime`, the seconds since its start, is lower than at the run before.
- **A healthy run without a limit** says `the memcached server at
  127.0.0.1:11211 gave its statistics; hits, misses, and evictions over
  60.000s`. With a limit, the message names each reading that has a limit in
  front of the message about receiving statistics and the measurement
  interval.
- **MMWatchdog reads at most 64 KiB of an answer.** MMWatchdog shows the server's
  answer with every character replaced that changes how text is shown, as for every
  check of a common service
  ([protocols and common server software](../../changing-mmwatchdog/design/checks.md#protocols-and-common-server-software)).

## Errors and what they mean

- **`check_groups.cache.checks.cache_answers_and_has_room.memcached: address
  127.0.0.1: missing port in address`.** The address has no port. Write the
  `memcached` value as host:port, such as `127.0.0.1:11211`.
- **`... memcached: port must be a number from 1 to 65535`.** The port is
  not an integer from 1 to 65535.
- **`check_groups.cache.time_limit_per_run: must exceed 200ms for the
  initial sample of the memcached server's counters`.** The first run asks
  the server twice, 200 ms apart. Give the check group a longer
  `time_limit_per_run`.
- **`dial tcp 127.0.0.1:11211: connect: connection refused`.** No program
  listens at `127.0.0.1:11211`. Start memcached, or correct the address.
- **`the connection to 127.0.0.1:11211 did not open within the time limit of the
  run`.** The connection did not open before the time limit of the run ended it.
- **`the server at 127.0.0.1:11211 did not answer within the time limit of
  the run`, or `... ended the connection before its answer was complete`.**
  The server is overloaded or hangs. The alert's body shows what the
  server sent until the timeout or connection closure.
- **`the server at 127.0.0.1:11211 did not answer with the statistics of a
  memcached server`.** Another program listens at `127.0.0.1:11211`, such as a Redis server. The alert's
  body shows the listening program's response, after `the server
  sent:`.
- **`the memcached server gave no limit_maxbytes`** (or `no
  curr_connections`, `no curr_items`, `no get_hits`, and so on). The run is
  unknown because a limited measurement needs the missing counter named
  in the error. A server that only speaks memcached's protocol, such as a
  proxy, can leave numbers out.
- **`the memcached server answered no gets in the last 60.000s, so
  cache_hit_percent cannot be measured`.** The run is unknown because a
  limit names the hit ratio, and the application asked the server for
  nothing in the time that the message names.

## Tested on

- **Go tests:** `TestMemcachedCheck` in `protocol_checks_test.go` runs the
  check against a stand-in server on the test machine. The test covers:
  - statistics that provide every measurement;
  - a limit that passes and a limit that fails;
  - the first run, with two counter readings;
  - a cold cache followed by a warm cache;
  - an interval without gets;
  - a server that started again;
  - a restarted server whose counters already exceed the previous values;
  - a server that gives no counters of gets;
  - a server that answers `ERROR` or another protocol.

  `TestTCPCheckSendsATextAndExpectsAReply` covers validation.
  `TestChecksOfServersThatDoNotAnswerAsExpected` checks a port where
  nothing listens.
- **Real servers:** the `services` suite (`service_scenarios.py`) gets the
  statistics of memcached as each distribution installs it, with a limit on
  `cache_used_percent`, and finds the check failed while memcached is
  stopped and healthy after it starts again. The latest run passed on
  [every target distribution](../../changing-mmwatchdog/testing.md#every-target-distribution)
  ([validation record](../../changing-mmwatchdog/validation.md)). On Debian 13, the suite
  also passed checks of `cached_items`, `cache_hits_per_second`,
  `cache_misses_per_second`, and `cache_evictions_per_second` from the real
  server. The Debian 13 run verified `cache_hit_percent` of 0 when every
  get misses and 100 when every get hits.
- **Not verified on a real node:** a server that answers a part and then
  waits. A Go test covers a server that sends a partial answer and then
  waits.

## Why it works this way

- **Without `bytes`, there is no `cache_used_percent` reading.** A missing
  counter does not mean zero use. A limit on `cache_used_percent` makes the
  run unknown with the missing counter named.

- **A full cache is not a failure by itself.** memcached makes room by
  removing old items, so the check fails on the cache only with a limit
  chosen by the person writing the check configuration.
- **The hit ratio covers the time since the run before,** not the time since
  the server started. A server that has run for weeks has a hit ratio
  since the server's start that hardly moves. Recent misses have too
  little effect on the lifetime ratio to clearly reveal a cold cache or
  an application change that causes misses all the time.
- **The hits, misses, and evictions are per second.** A limit then means the
  maximum or minimum hits, misses, or evictions per second, whatever the
  check group's `check_every` is.
- **A time without gets has no hit ratio, not one of 0 or 100.** Reporting
  0 percent or 100 percent would invent a hit ratio for an interval with
  no gets.
- **The address has no default port.** A reader sees on each check where it
  connects.
- **The module is named for memcached,** as every core module that checks a
  common service is named for the tool. The name
  helps a reader recognize the service being checked.
